title: Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization via Privileged Self-Distillation

paper.title: Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization via Privileged Self-Distillation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Recent advances in post-training Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) or On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD).
While OPSD provides dense, logit-level supervision, it inherently suffers from exposure bias due to the privileged information of the self-teacher.
In multi-turn agentic settings, this leads to reasoning route convergence and the loss of clear optimization directions.
To tackle these challenges, we introduce Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization (CRPO), which reformulates agentic OPSD from a contrastive learning perspective.
By leveraging predictive entropy to distinguish between positive positions (reflective exploration) and negative positions (exposure bias), CRPO conducts group-wise contrast to preserve reliable, fine-grained optimization signals.
Extensive evaluations across 13 challenging reasoning and deep-search benchmarks demonstrate that CRPO consistently outperforms existing reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines, significantly enhancing training stability and generalization in long-horizon interactions.

Meituan {wuxingjian02, guolinsen}@meituan.com 1 Introduction Recent advances in post-training Large Language Models (LLM) gradually converge along two complementary paradigms. Among them, Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) ( DeepSeek-AI 2026 ; Dong et al. 2025d ) optimizes policies against verifiable outcome-level feedback, yielding accurate but sparse rewards, where a single scalar supervises an entire generation with coarse-grained credit assignment on intermediate steps. To tackle this, On-Policy Distillation (OPD) ( Song and Zheng 2026 ; Li et al. 2026b ) and On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) ( Zhao et al. 2026 ; Hübotter et al. 2026 ) supply dense, logit-level guidance from a stronger teacher model. We focus on OPSD, which provides a self-improved mechanism possessing both dense supervision and low computation cost. However, its guidance is inherently privileged, as the self-teacher model benefits from information advantage, and thus can be overconfident at positions where the student model is genuinely uncertain, leading to exposure bias ( Yang et al. 2026 ) . This problem is further amplified in agentic post-training due to the multi-turn interactions with external environments, and we attribute it into two key phenomena: [1] Self-teacher’s reasoning route converges in interaction turns and [2] Optimization directions lose in multi-turn distillation . Figure 1: Position-level entropy along a student trajectory on a deep-search task in GAIA, compared with that of a privileged self-teacher prompted with a few demonstrations. A systematic statistical validation across all training rollouts is provided in Appendix D.1 . [Phenomenon-1] Self-teacher’s reasoning route converges in interaction turns. Figure 1 visualizes the position-level entropy along a student trajectory on a deep-search task, together with the entropy of a self-teacher obtained by prompting the same model with a few demonstrations. After each tool call, the freshly introduced external information drives the student’s entropy sharply upward. Under these circumstances with high uncertainty, it is observed that the privileged self-teacher may follow the reasoning routes of demonstrated cases to improve its confidence , which leads to a significant entropy drop at these positions. This potentially hinders the model’s generalization capability. [Phenomenon-2] Optimization directions lose in multi-turn distillation. Pure OPSD methods ( Zhao et al. 2026 ; Hübotter et al. 2026 ) utilize the KL-divergence to integrate the internalized reward signals from the privileged self-teacher, which is effective in single-turn tasks. However, in multi-turn long-horizon interactions, the reward signals are volunerable due to the introduction of external information. As above-mentioned, the teacher model is subjected to exposure bias, yielding to unreliable position-level supervision signals. As presented in Figure 2 , compared with RLVR methods like GRPO ( DeepSeek-AI 2026 ) and ARPO ( Dong et al. 2025d ) , the reward curve of OPSD exhibits a fluctuating pattern while the KL-Divergence increases sharply, which indicates that the model is misled by the privileged self-teacher and fails to capture reward signals. Figure 2: The Reward and KL-Divergence (token-average) of GRPO, ARPO, and OPSD during agentic post-training. Based on the observations, we think the core problem is that the position-level supervision signals are unreliable in agentic post-training. To tackle above challenges, we think the pivots lie in: [1] selectively distilling key positions and punishing ones with exposure bias , and [2] focusing on relatively advantageous positions to preserve clear optimization directions . Though some existing studies ( Yang et al. 2026 ; Lu et al. 2026 ; Pan et al. 2026 ) attempt to address the first problem, their solutions tend to rely on using self-distillation signals to control the update magnitude of RLVR, or to weightsum with RLVR’s optimization objective. Since they take two separate frameworks into account, additional computational overhead is introduced. In contrast, we provide a solution to enhance the OPSD itself. To address the above-mentioned challenges, we introduce CRPO , a Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization method for agentic OPSD. In CRPO, we reformulate the OPSD framework from a contrastive learning perspective. Specifically, we treat ♣ the original context and the context with privileged information as two views (i.e., the original view and the augmented view), ♠ the policy model as the encoder, ♥ the output logits as the representations, and ♠ the negative KL-divergence as the similarity function. The objective is to perform distillation at positions that improve the model’s generalization (positive pairs) while penalizing positions where exposure bias occurs (negative pairs). To ensure clear optimization signals, we draw inspiration from the group-wise scheme of GRPO, conducting group-wise contrast across positions and encouraging relatively advantageous positions. Our contributions are summarized as: ❶ We propose CRPO, an OPSD algorithm from a contrastive learning perspective, which enhances the training stability and performance in agentic post-training. ❷ We use predictive-entropy to classify the positive and negative position and conduct group-wise contrast to preserve clear optimization directions. ❸ Beyond heurisitc motivation, the theoretical formula of CRPO is demonstrated equivalent to possess logit-wise credit assignment with a soft gate–see Appendix C . ❹ Extensive evaluations on 13 challenging benchmarks show that CRPO consistently outperforms existing RL baselines across diverse reasoning and agentic tasks. 2 Related Works 2.1 Agentic Reinforcement Learning Recently, Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) ( Lambert et al. 2025 ; DeepSeek-AI 2026 ; Yu et al. 2025 ) has achieved progress in enhancing reasoning tasks ( Qiao et al. 2024 ; Shao et al. 2024 ; Team 2025c ) . Extending it to agentic settings, where models interact with external tools over multiple turns ( Qian et al. 2025 ; Dong et al. 2025c ; Team 2025a ) , introduces new challenges such as long-horizon credit assignment, high uncertainty after each tool call, and compounding errors across turns. Recent efforts attempt to address these from several angles: adaptive exploration strategies ( Dong et al. 2025d ; Dong et al. 2025a ) that exploit entropy spikes after tool interactions to encourage step-level sampling at high-uncertainty positions, and step-wise advantage attribution that internalizes the contribution of individual tool-use actions within the trajectory-level reward ( Wang et al. 2025 ; Jin et al. 2025 ) . Despite these advances, existing agentic RL methods rely solely on sparse outcome-level rewards and lack dense token-level signals, limiting sample efficiency and intermediate-step guidance. 2.2 On-Policy Self-Distillation On-policy distillation (OPD) ( Song and Zheng 2026 ; Li et al. 2026b ; Hou et al. 2026 ; Fang et al. 2026 ) provides dense, logit-level supervision by aligning the student’s distribution with a stronger teacher at every position. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) ( Zhao et al. 2026 ; Hübotter et al. 2026 ; Wang et al. 2026b ) simplifies this by letting a single model serve as both student and teacher, with the teacher granted privileged information to produce the dense signal at no extra model cost. OPSD ( Zhao et al. 2026 ) first introduces this self-distilled framework for single-turn reasoning. SDPO ( Hübotter et al. 2026 ) frames self-distillation as an RL objective, using the teacher-student KL divergence as a dense reward signal. Several works further explore hybrid methods combining OPSD with RLVR. RLSD ( Yang et al. 2026 ) uses the self-distillation signal to modulate RLVR policy gradient updates. SDAR ( Lu et al. 2026 ) jointly optimizes an RL objective and a distillation objective in multi-turn agentic settings. Skill-SD ( Wang et al. 2026a ) applies skill as the privileged information in agentic settings. RLCSD ( Pan et al. 2026 ) introduces contrastive signals to distinguish stylistic differences between successful and unsuccessful trajectories in reasoning tasks. HDPO ( Ding 2026 ) combines multiple supervision sources via privileged self-distillation into a unified policy optimization objective. Our proposed CRPO, reformulates OPSD from a contrastive perspective ( Chen et al. 2020 ; He et al. 2020 ) , controling fine-grained distillation and preserving clear advantageous signals. Given an initial task description x x , we consider the agentic scenario where an LLM π θ \pi_{\theta} interacts with the environment through external tools, obtains observations from the tools, and then makes responses. Note that this process involves external tokens (e.g., searched information), which only serve as the context and do not provide optimization signals, so that we only formulate the valid response tokens for notational simplicity: y i = ( y i , 1 , ⋯ , y i , t , ⋯ , y i , c i ) ∼ π θ ( ⋅ | x ) , \displaystyle y_{i}=(y_{i,1},\cdots,y_{i,t},\cdots,y_{i,c_{i}})\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x), (1) where y i y_{i} denotes the sampled sequence and c i c_{i} denotes the length. Total G \mathrm{G} rollouts are sampled per question x x . In the context of OPSD, the student and teacher share the same policy model π θ \pi_{\theta} . At each position t t , the student model’s context of the i i -th sampled rollout is defined as: S i , t = ( x , y i , < t ) , \displaystyle S_{i,t}=(x,y_{i,<t}), (2) and the self-teacher model’s context is formulated as: T i , t = ( x , f , y i , < t ) , \displaystyle T_{i,t}=(x,f,y_{i,<t}), (3) User: <question> Reference solution: <ref_trajectory> Environmental info: <env_feedback> Assistant: <student_response> Table 1: Self-teacher prompt template. where f f is the feedback, which is organized from the student’s own rollouts, covering the reference successful trajectories from the same group, and the environmental feedbacks such as the compile information of code interpreter.
